newsitem.title: FINLAND: EMU wobbles abroad not seen denting Finland's will.
newsitem.headline: EMU wobbles abroad not seen denting Finland's will.

text.p: It may be going too far to joke of a single European currency made up of just Finland and Luxembourg -- but economists say current upsets are unlikely to sway Finland's will to join.

But they warn that if Sweden were to opt out of the January 1999 launch of EMU, debate on the merits of the move would heat up at home. And any broad market volatility triggered by EMU-related political problems in France and Germany would undoubtedly have a domestic impact.
"I don't think (current upsets) will alter Finland's position," said Kirsi Hokka at Handelsbanken. "What will be affected is the domestic discussion."

In the short term, few believe louder opposition voices would threaten any change of course for Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's pro-EMU coalition government, which has a 141-seat majority in the 200-seat house.

A decision by Sweden to remain out of EMU would be no surprise for Finnish markets, although industry has warned it would give some of the country's keenest rivals -- especially in forestry -- exchange-rate flexibility which Finland would have lost.
It would also make Finland the only Nordic European Union member aiming to get on board.
Amid a broadly bumpy markets ride, the markka bond yield spread over German bunds would be in for a more elastic spell, analysts said.
Tarja Heinonen at Postipankki saw scope for it to widen to near 50 basis points, snapping back towards its current 30 bps level in a short time -- maybe as little as a week.
"A spread (Finland 2006 over 2007 Bunds) in excess of 50 basis points is a horror scenario, but we may easily climb over 40 bps," said OKOBANK's Teppo Koivisto.

But for now, Finnish markets seem to share the view of a Finnish member of the EU's monetary committee, who said on Thursday that the current EMU uproar would prove to be one of several storms in a teacup.
Despite broad bond market nerves, an issue on Thursday of Finland's main benchmark bond attracted record volume.

"I think we will see similar uncertainty factors cropping up from time to time; sometimes they might last a week, sometimes over a month or two, but then things will settle down and the markets will focus on something else," said Koivisto.
Hokka pointed out that Finnish markets are also supported by a belief in the government's determination to keep the economy fit with or without the EMU criteria as a finishing line.
Nonetheless, if future developments point to any delay in the single currency, she said Finnish and Irish markets would be more noticeably hit as operators unwind convergence positions.
